unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Measure temperature, pulse, and respirations accurately using the correct site, instrument, and technique.
- Recognize normal ranges and identify abnormal findings for temperature, pulse, and respirations.
- Report abnormal findings promptly and escalate to licensed clinical staff according to office policy.
- Apply infection-control practices when using, cleaning, and disinfecting measurement equipment.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Your body usually runs at about 98.6°F, like a thermostat set to a comfortable room temperature. It can drift a little higher or lower and still be fine.

### Question 2

A fever is when your body temperature climbs to 100.4°F or higher, like a warning light telling us the body is fighting something.

### Question 3

If your body cools below 95°F it is like a house losing its heat on a freezing night, which can be dangerous, so we tell the nurse or provider right away.

### Question 4

Measuring deep inside the body is like reading the temperature at the very center of a warm room, which is warmer than the air near the doorway.

### Question 5

The skin under your arm is like the outside edge of a warm room, which is a little cooler than the center, so the number reads a bit lower.

### Question 6

Just like you would wait for hot soup to stop warming your mouth, we wait a little while after eating or drinking so the thermometer reads your real body temperature.

### Question 7

The most accurate temperature is read from deep inside the body, like checking the oven's own thermometer rather than guessing from the heat near the door.

### Question 8

The ear canal is a little curvy, so we gently pull the ear up and back to make the path straighter, like straightening a garden hose so water flows right.

### Question 9

A forehead thermometer glides across your forehead like a tiny scanner to read the warmth of a blood vessel just under the skin.

### Question 10

Old glass thermometers had a silvery liquid inside that is poisonous if it spills, so we now use safer digital thermometers instead.

### Question 11

A fresh cover is like a fresh glove or a clean cup between each person, so no one shares germs.

### Question 12

We clean the thermometer after every single person, the same way we wash a cup before the next person drinks from it, because germs can hide where we cannot see them.

### Question 13

We write down exactly what the thermometer says, and where we measured it, right away, like writing down a recipe step so we do not forget it.

### Question 14

If a measuring cup suddenly said there was a whole gallon when the jug looks nearly empty, you would measure again before believing it; we do the same with an odd temperature.

### Question 15

When the temperature alarm goes high, we pass the number to the nurse or doctor so they can decide what to do, just like calling an adult when a child's temperature climbs.

### Question 16

Your body's inner temperature goes up and down a little through the day, like the sun's warmth changing from a cool morning to a warm afternoon.

### Question 17

Febrile is the fancy word for running a fever, and afebrile means no fever.

### Question 18

Pyrexia is just another word doctors and nurses use for a fever.

### Question 19

An oral thermometer must sit quietly under the tongue, so it is not used for a baby who cannot hold it there; we choose a different spot instead.

### Question 20

We tuck the thermometer in a dry armpit and have the patient hug their arm down, like closing a lid so the warmth stays in until it is ready.

### Question 21

The thermometer beeps when it is done, like a kitchen timer going off, so we wait for the beep before reading the number.

### Question 22

A very young or very old body can be more sensitive to heat and cold, so we pay extra attention to their temperature numbers.

### Question 23

A body temperature that low is like an engine running out of heat, and we call for help right away instead of waiting to see what happens.

### Question 24

Our job is to report the number clearly, like delivering a message, and let the doctor decide what it means and what to do.

### Question 25

We glide the forehead thermometer over clean, dry skin following the instructions, like moving a scanner smoothly over a barcode.

### Question 26

Right after sipping hot tea, your mouth is warmer than the rest of you, so the thermometer would read too high until it cools back down.

### Question 27

37 degrees Celsius and 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit are the same temperature, just like the same distance can be written in inches or centimeters.

### Question 28

Only one of these numbers is like a red warning light, and that is the 103°F fever, so that is the one we report.

### Question 29

There is no single magic number; a normal temperature is a comfortable zone that shifts a little from person to person and hour to hour.

### Question 30

When your body heats up to fight an illness, your heart works faster, like an engine revving higher to cool the car down.

### Question 31

If the thermometer and the patient are telling different stories, we measure again and tell the nurse about both, so nothing important is missed.

### Question 32

A grown-up's heart usually beats between 60 and 100 times each minute while resting.

### Question 33

Bradycardia means the heart is beating slowly, fewer than 60 times a minute.

### Question 34

Tachycardia means the heart is racing, beating more than 100 times a minute.

### Question 35

The wrist pulse sits on the thumb side, where you can feel the beat right under the skin.

### Question 36

Your thumb has its own heartbeat, so if you press with it you might count yourself instead of the patient, so we use the pointer and middle fingers.

### Question 37

When the beats are uneven, we count for a whole minute so we do not miss any, like counting every jellybean instead of guessing.

### Question 38

If the rhythm is steady, we can count for half a minute and double it, like counting cars for half a minute and multiplying to know the full minute.

### Question 39

The apical pulse is the heart's own sound, so we listen with a stethoscope right over the heart, like putting an ear to a door.

### Question 40

For babies, it is easier and more accurate to listen right over the heart than to find a tiny wrist beat.

### Question 41

When we check a pulse we ask three things: how fast, how steady, and how strong each beat feels.

### Question 42

If the beats are uneven like a drummer missing steps, we count carefully and tell the nurse or doctor, because it could matter.

### Question 43

The neck pulse is checked gently and on one side only, because squeezing both sides could cut off the brain's blood supply.

### Question 44

If we cannot feel the wrist beat on one side, we try the other wrist and tell the nurse, rather than guessing.

### Question 45

We write the exact number and where we felt it, right away, so the record is true and complete.

### Question 46

A pulse deficit is when the heart beats more times than we can feel at the wrist, like a pump that squeezes but not every squeeze reaches the hose.

### Question 47

Your heart beats faster when you run or climb stairs because your body needs more oxygen, and it slows back down when you rest.

### Question 48

A fit heart is like a strong pump that moves a lot of water with each squeeze, so it does not need to pump as often.

### Question 49

We use the soft pads of two fingers and press gently, like feeling for a faint knock on a door without pushing it shut.

### Question 50

If you squeeze a garden hose too tightly, the water stops; pressing too hard on a pulse does the same thing.

### Question 51

We let the patient sit and relax first, like letting a car engine idle before checking the gauges, so we read the true resting number.

### Question 52

The heart's true beat can sometimes be too faint to feel at the wrist, so listening to the heart can give a higher number than the wrist.

### Question 53

A pulse that feels faint and thin, like a weak trickle from a tap, is a sign to call the nurse or doctor.

### Question 54

A pulse that feels extra forceful is like a water pipe surging, and we let the doctor know so it can be checked.

### Question 55

For a routine check we use the easy wrist pulse; the neck and other spots are saved for special situations.

### Question 56

In an emergency we feel the neck pulse because it is a big, strong pulse near the heart that we can usually find.

### Question 57

You can feel your heartbeat in several places, and the wrist is one of the easiest spots.

### Question 58

In a healthy steady heart, every beat shows up at the wrist, so counting the wrist beats tells us the heart rate.

### Question 59

A resting heart rate over 100 is like an engine idling too fast, so we tell the nurse or doctor to check it out.

### Question 60

A regular pulse is like a metronome or a steady drumbeat, each beat evenly spaced.

### Question 61

We counted 19 beats in a quarter of a minute, so we multiply by 4 to find the whole minute: 76 beats.

### Question 62

A grown-up at rest usually breathes about 12 to 20 times each minute.

### Question 63

Tachypnea means breathing too fast, more than 20 times a minute at rest.

### Question 64

Bradypnea means breathing too slowly, fewer than 12 times a minute.

### Question 65

Apnea means breathing pauses for a little while, like a movie that pauses before starting again.

### Question 66

If someone knows you are counting their breaths, they might breathe differently without meaning to, so we count quietly without saying anything.

### Question 67

We keep holding the wrist as if still counting the pulse, while we quietly watch the chest rise and fall so the patient breathes naturally.

### Question 68

We count breaths for a whole minute, like timing an entire song, so we do not miss any slow or uneven breaths.

### Question 69

One breath is the chest going up and coming back down once, like a balloon filling and emptying.

### Question 70

We watch the chest go up and down, like watching a balloon slowly inflate and deflate, to count each breath.

### Question 71

Dyspnea means it feels hard to breathe, like trying to run after being out of breath.

### Question 72

Breathing 28 times a minute at rest is too fast, like panting, so we tell the nurse or doctor right away.

### Question 73

Babies breathe quickly, like little engines running fast, and that faster rate is normal for them.

### Question 74

When you run, your body needs more air, so you breathe faster; when you rest, your breathing slows back down.

### Question 75

Besides counting breaths, we notice whether breathing is steady, deep or shallow, and easy or hard.

### Question 76

Shallow breathing is like taking tiny sips of air instead of a full drink.

### Question 77

When someone is struggling to breathe, we get help right away, like calling for help when someone cannot catch their breath.

### Question 78

It is hard to count natural breaths while someone is chatting, because talking changes how they breathe.

### Question 79

We really count the breaths, like counting steps, instead of guessing, because guessing can be wrong.

### Question 80

Only the struggling, uneven breathing is a red flag; the other options are normal breathing.

### Question 81

Orthopnea means a person can breathe more easily sitting up than lying down, like needing more pillows to sleep comfortably.

### Question 82

We write the exact number we counted, plus a note if the breathing looked unusual, so the record is complete.

### Question 83

When the body heats up with a fever, it works harder and breathes faster, like a machine running hot and spinning its fan faster.

### Question 84

If the patient starts talking, we pause like a paused stopwatch and start again when they are quiet, so the count stays true.

### Question 85

Breathing that stops and starts unevenly is like a flickering light, and we tell the nurse or doctor so they can check it.

### Question 86

Breathing only 8 times a minute is too slow, like an engine almost stalling, so we tell the nurse or doctor.

### Question 87

New babies breathe very quickly, 30 to 60 times a minute, which is normal for them.

### Question 88

Your breathing slows down when you sleep, like a car idling gently overnight.

### Question 89

Normal breathing is calm and quiet, like a gentle breeze, not loud or hard work.

### Question 90

Our job is to hand the number to the doctor or nurse, like passing a note, and let them decide what it means and what to do.
